monuments.name: Hagia Sophia (Great Church)
monuments.builderName: Justinian; architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus

phases.t: first church dedicated under Constantius II
burned in the Nika riot; rebuilding begun 23 February

monuments.summary: The first Great Church, a timber-roofed basilica, was dedicated on 15 February 360 under Constantius II; it burned on 20 June 404 in the riots after John Chrysostom's exile. Theodosius II's rebuilding (dedicated 10 October 415; its propylon with a frieze of lambs survives) burned on 14 January 532 in the Nika riot. Justinian began the present church on 23 February 532, designed by the mathematicians Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, and dedicated it on 27 December 537: a dome about 31 m across, rising on pendentives over a 70 m nave flanked by semi-domes. Weakened by earthquakes in 553 and 557, the dome fell on 7 May 558; Isidore the Younger rebuilt it about 6 m higher, and the church was rededicated on 24 December 562, the occasion of Paul the Silentiary's ekphrasis. Procopius (Buildings 1.1) wrote that the dome seemed suspended from heaven on a golden chain. Partial collapses followed in 989 and 1346; it became a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934 and a mosque again in 2020.

monuments.name: Hagia Irene
monuments.summary: The church of Holy Peace, one of the oldest in the city, served as cathedral before the first Hagia Sophia was completed and lay within the same precinct. The Second Ecumenical Council met here in 381. Burned in the Nika riot of 532, it was rebuilt by Justinian as a domed basilica; after the earthquake of 740 Constantine V rebuilt it again, and its apse still carries the plain iconoclast cross of that rebuilding. The Ottomans used it as an arsenal, so it was never converted to a mosque.

monuments.name: Church of the Holy Apostles
monuments.builderName: Constantine (mausoleum); Constantius II; rebuilt by Justinian

phases.t: relics of Andrew and Luke deposited

monuments.summary: Constantine built his mausoleum here, where his porphyry sarcophagus lay among twelve cenotaphs of the apostles, making him, as Eusebius (Life 4.58-60) implies, the thirteenth. Constantius II added a cruciform church and brought the relics of Timothy (356) and of Andrew and Luke (357). Justinian rebuilt it as a five-domed cross (completed 550), the model for San Marco in Venice; emperors were buried here until the 11th century. Mehmed II demolished it in 1461-62 to build the Fatih Mosque on its site.

monuments.name: Theotokos Chalkoprateia
monuments.summary: A basilica of the Virgin in the coppersmiths' quarter just west of Hagia Sophia, founded in the mid-5th century (attributed to Pulcheria or to Verina) to house the Virgin's girdle. It was the second most important Marian shrine of the city after Blachernae. Ruins survive near the Zeynep Sultan Mosque.

monuments.name: St Polyeuktos
monuments.summary: Built in 524-527 by Anicia Juliana, the richest woman in the empire, granddaughter of Valentinian III and great-granddaughter of Theodosius II, as a statement of dynastic pride against the upstart Justin and Justinian. About 52 m square, it was the largest church in the city until Hagia Sophia, possibly domed, decorated with peacocks, vine scrolls and carved marble of Persian inspiration; its 76-line dedicatory epigram, preserved in the Palatine Anthology (1.10), was carved round the nave. Harrison argued its dimensions reproduced Solomon's Temple in royal cubits. Gregory of Tours tells how she gilded the roof rather than hand her gold to Justinian. Excavated at Saraçhane in 1964-69 by R. M. Harrison and N. Fıratlı; its 'Pilastri Acritani' were looted to Venice in 1204.

monuments.name: Saints Sergius and Bacchus (Küçük Ayasofya)

phases.t: Pope Vigilius takes refuge in the adjoining church

monuments.summary: Built by Justinian and Theodora between 527 and 536 beside the Palace of Hormisdas where Justinian had lived as heir: a domed octagon set irregularly inside a square, a laboratory for the ideas of Hagia Sophia. The dedicatory inscription in its frieze names both rulers and calls Theodora 'crowned by God'. It may have served Theodora's miaphysite monks. In 551 Pope Vigilius took refuge in the adjoining church of Saints Peter and Paul. It became a mosque around 1504-1512.

monuments.name: St John of Stoudios
monuments.summary: The oldest substantially surviving church in the city, a basilica built about 454-463 by the patrician Stoudios, consul in 454, near the Golden Gate, with a monastery that under Theodore the Studite in the 9th century led the defence of icons. It became the İmrahor İlyas Bey Mosque in 1486 and, after centuries in ruins, was reopened as a mosque in 2024.

monuments.name: Theotokos of the Spring (Pege)
monuments.summary: A church built by Justinian (Procopius Buildings 1.3; later tradition adds that he used materials left over from Hagia Sophia) around a healing spring outside the land walls near the Gate of Pege, which took its name. The present Greek Orthodox church at Balıklı was rebuilt in the 1830s.

monuments.name: Theotokos of Blachernae

phases.t: Hagia Soros rotunda for the robe
icon paraded on the walls in the Avar siege

monuments.summary: Built by Pulcheria and Marcian from about 450 and completed by Leo I by a holy spring at the north end of the city; a rotunda (Hagia Soros) was added in 473-474 for the Virgin's robe brought from Palestine. During the Avar-Persian siege of 626 the patriarch Sergius carried her icon round the walls, and the city credited her with its deliverance, celebrated in the Akathistos hymn. Heraclius then extended the walls to enclose it. It burned in 1434; a small church of 1867 marks the spring.

monuments.name: Great Palace

phases.t: burned in part in the Nika riot; rebuilt by Justinian

monuments.summary: The imperial residence founded by Constantine between the Hippodrome and the Sea of Marmara, an agglomeration of halls, churches, courts and gardens descending on terraces to the sea, rebuilt and expanded for eight centuries. Constantine's Daphne palace adjoined the Hippodrome through the Kathisma box; the Chalke gate opened on the Augusteion; Justin II added the Chrysotriklinos throne room (565-578). The Komnenoi moved to Blachernae in the 12th century and it was ruined by 1453. Excavations since 1935 (Walker Trust, Turkish teams) have uncovered only fragments.

monuments.name: Chalke Gate
monuments.summary: The monumental vestibule of the Great Palace on the Augusteion, named for its bronze roof. Burned in the Nika riot, it was rebuilt by Justinian with mosaics of Belisarius' victories over the Vandals and Goths and Justinian and Theodora receiving the spoils (Procopius Buildings 1.10). An icon of Christ over its door was, according to later sources, the first target of iconoclasm in 726 or 730.

monuments.name: Boukoleon Palace and Harbour
monuments.summary: The seaside section of the Great Palace with its private harbour on the Marmara, named after a statue of a bull fighting a lion. Traditionally begun under Theodosius II, it was fortified by Nikephoros II in the 10th century. A façade with marble window frames survives in the sea wall.

monuments.name: Peristyle mosaic of the Great Palace
monuments.summary: A floor mosaic of about 1,870 square metres from a peristyle courtyard of the Great Palace, with hunting, pastoral and mythological scenes in a classical style on a white ground. Found in 1935-38; the Austrian excavations of 1983-97 favoured a date in the Justinianic period, though dates between about 450 and the 7th century have been argued. It is now displayed in situ in the Great Palace Mosaic Museum.

monuments.name: Hippodrome of Constantinople
monuments.summary: Begun by Septimius Severus when he rebuilt Byzantium after 196 and completed by Constantine for the city's dedication on 11 May 330, about 450 m long and 120 m wide, seating perhaps 30,000-50,000 (estimates up to 100,000 exist). The emperor appeared to the people in the Kathisma box linked to the palace, making it the arena of political acclamation and riot; in January 532 the Nika revolt ended with Belisarius and Mundus trapping and killing about 30,000 people inside (Procopius). The spina held the Obelisk of Theodosius, the Serpent Column, the Walled Obelisk and the bronze horses now at San Marco, taken in 1204. The SW curve (sphendone) survives on massive substructures; the At Meydanı preserves the track.

monuments.name: Obelisk of Theodosius
monuments.summary: The upper part (about 20 m) of an obelisk of Thutmose III from the temple of Karnak, shipped to Constantinople under Constantius II or Julian and erected in 390 on the spina of the Hippodrome by the city prefect Proculus for Theodosius I. Latin and Greek verses on the base boast that it was raised in 30 (or 32) days; its reliefs show Theodosius and his court in the Kathisma presiding over the races and receiving barbarian tribute.

monuments.name: Serpent Column
monuments.summary: The bronze base of the gold tripod dedicated at Delphi by the Greek cities after Plataea in 479 BC, three intertwined serpents inscribed with the names of 31 states. Constantine brought it to the Hippodrome. The heads were broken off around 1700; part of one jaw is in the Istanbul Archaeological Museum.

monuments.name: Augusteion
monuments.summary: The colonnaded square south of Hagia Sophia, named after the porphyry column with the statue of the Augusta Helena. The Senate house closed its east side, the Chalke gate and Baths of Zeuxippus its south, the Milion stood at its west corner. Justinian rebuilt it after the Nika riot and set up his bronze equestrian column in it in 543.

monuments.name: Senate House (Augusteion)
monuments.summary: One of Constantinople's two Senate houses, on the east side of the Augusteion. It burned in 404 in the riots over Chrysostom; Zosimus (5.24) says the bronze statues of Zeus of Dodona and Athena of Lindos survived miraculously. Burned again in 532 and rebuilt by Justinian.

monuments.name: Baths of Zeuxippus
monuments.summary: Public baths begun by Septimius Severus and completed by Constantine at the NE end of the Hippodrome, famous for about 80 bronze statues of gods, heroes, poets and orators, catalogued in verse by Christodorus of Coptus (Palatine Anthology book 2). They burned with the collection in the Nika riot; Justinian partly rebuilt them, and they later served as a prison and silk workshop. Excavated in 1927-28.

monuments.name: Milion

phases.t: statues of Justin II and Sophia added

monuments.summary: The zero milestone of the empire, built by Constantine in imitation of Rome's Miliarium Aureum: a domed tetrapylon from which distances on the roads were measured, crowned with statues of Constantine and Helena holding a cross. Statues of Justin II and Sophia were added. A single marble pier was found in 1967-68 at the start of the Divanyolu, near the Basilica Cistern.

monuments.name: Mese
monuments.summary: The colonnaded main street, about 25 m wide with its porticoes, running from the Milion west through the Forum of Constantine and the Forum of Theodosius to the Philadelphion, where it forked: one branch NW past the Holy Apostles to the Gate of Charisius, the other SW through the Forum Bovis and the Forum of Arcadius to the Golden Gate, the route of triumphs. The Divanyolu and Ordu Caddesi follow its first stretch. The line given is schematic.

monuments.name: Basilica Cistern
monuments.summary: A covered reservoir about 138 by 65 m under the Stoa Basilica, rebuilt by Justinian after the Nika riot, perhaps on an earlier cistern. 336 columns in 12 rows of 28, many reused, support brick vaults; it held about 80,000 cubic metres for the Great Palace. Two Medusa heads lie as column bases. The Ottomans drew water from it through wells without knowing its extent until Pierre Gilles explored it in 1545.

monuments.name: Stoa Basilica
monuments.summary: A colonnaded square west of the Augusteion housing law courts, booksellers and the imperial library. The library, said to hold 120,000 books including a 36 m gut-roll of Homer, burned in the fire of 475 under Basiliscus; the stoa burned again in 532 and the cistern below was rebuilt by Justinian.

monuments.name: Cistern of Philoxenus (Binbirdirek)
monuments.summary: A covered cistern of about 64 by 56 m with 224 columns, each made of two shafts stacked, probably of the 5th century and connected with the nearby palaces of Lausus and Antiochus; tradition names a senator Philoxenus of Constantine's time. The Turkish name means 'thousand and one columns'.

monuments.name: Cistern of Aetius
monuments.summary: An open-air reservoir about 244 by 85 m built in 421 by the urban prefect Aetius near the Gate of Charisius, one of three great open cisterns that stored the water of the aqueduct system within the Theodosian walls. It is now the Vefa sports stadium in Karagümrük.

monuments.name: Cistern of Aspar
monuments.summary: An open cistern 152 m square and about 10 m deep built in 459 by the Alan general Aspar, kingmaker of Marcian and Leo I, who was murdered by Leo in 471. It lies beside the Yavuz Selim Mosque and was used for gardens (Çukurbostan, 'sunken garden').

monuments.name: Cistern of Mocius
monuments.summary: The largest of the open cisterns, about 170 by 147 m, built under Anastasius I (491-518) near the church of St Mocius on the seventh hill, in the Altımermer quarter. Used later as orchards.

monuments.name: Forum of Constantine

phases.t: statue of Athena smashed by a mob

monuments.summary: A circular (or oval) colonnaded forum outside the old Severan wall of Byzantium, dedicated with the city on 11 May 330, with two monumental arches on the Mese, a Senate house on its north side and a collection of statues from across the Greek world, Pheidias' Athena among them according to later sources. Its centre was the porphyry column of Constantine.

monuments.name: Column of Constantine (Çemberlitaş)

phases.t: iron hoops added after a fire

monuments.summary: A shaft of Egyptian porphyry drums on a tall base, still about 35 m high, crowned by a bronze statue of Constantine with a radiate crown in the guise of Apollo-Helios. Tradition held that the Palladium of Troy and Rome and Christian relics were buried in its base. The statue fell in a gale in 1106 and Manuel I replaced it with a cross. After a fire in 1779 the Ottomans bound the cracked drums with iron hoops, hence 'the hooped stone'.

monuments.name: Forum of Theodosius (Forum Tauri)

phases.t: column fragments reused in the Beyazıt bath

monuments.summary: The largest forum of the city, laid out by Theodosius I in 393 on the old Forum Tauri, with a triumphal arch whose columns were carved like knotted tree trunks (remains on Ordu Caddesi) and a column with a spiral relief of his victories, modelled on Trajan's. The column's statue fell in the earthquake of 480 and was replaced by one of Anastasius in 506. The site is Beyazıt Square.

monuments.name: Philadelphion
monuments.summary: The square at the fork of the Mese, named for a statue group of Constantine's sons embracing in brotherly love; the porphyry Tetrarchs set into the corner of San Marco in Venice, looted in 1204, came from here, and a missing foot fragment was found in excavations near the Bodrum Mosque in the 1960s.

monuments.name: Capitolium
monuments.summary: Constantine's Capitol at the fork of the Mese, a temple of the Roman type in name at least. In 425 Theodosius II established the public 'university' in its exedrae, with 31 salaried chairs: 10 Latin and 10 Greek grammarians, 3 Latin and 5 Greek rhetors, 1 philosopher and 2 jurists.

monuments.name: Forum Bovis
monuments.summary: A forum in the Lycus valley (Aksaray) on the SW branch of the Mese, named for a great bronze ox head that later tradition described as a furnace used to burn criminals and martyrs.

monuments.name: Forum and Column of Arcadius (Xerolophos)
monuments.summary: A forum on the seventh hill with a column begun by Arcadius in 403 and completed by Theodosius II in 421, whose spiral relief commemorated the expulsion and massacre of Gainas' Goths in 400. Its reliefs are known from drawings such as the Freshfield Album (1574); the shaft was taken down in 1715 after earthquake damage, leaving only the base in Cerrahpaşa.

monuments.name: Column of Marcian (Kıztaşı)
monuments.summary: A granite column with a Corinthian capital and Victories on the base, set up by the urban prefect Tatianus for Marcian in 450-452, as its Latin inscription says. Its Turkish name, 'maiden's stone', comes from the Victory figures.

monuments.name: Column of Justinian
monuments.summary: A brick column sheathed in bronze set up in the Augusteion in 543, carrying a colossal bronze equestrian statue of Justinian in Achilles' armour holding a globe, facing east towards Persia (Procopius Buildings 1.2). Drawn by Cyriac of Ancona in the 1430s; the Ottomans took it down in the early 16th century and Pierre Gilles saw the fragments being melted.

monuments.name: Aqueduct of Valens (Bozdoğan Kemeri)
monuments.summary: The bridge, about 920 m surviving of an original 971 m and up to 29 m high, that carried the city's water across the valley between the third and fourth hills, completed under Valens in 368; a great nymphaeum was dedicated in 373. It was the terminal of the longest water supply system of antiquity, which the survey of Crow, Bardill and Bayliss traced for more than 400 km of channels into Thrace, extended in the 5th century. The Avars cut it in 626; Constantine V restored it after the drought of 765.

monuments.name: Harbour of Theodosius (Eleutherios)
monuments.summary: The largest harbour on the Marmara shore, built under Theodosius I at the mouth of the Lycus valley, used for the grain fleets and gradually silted up. Excavations for the Marmaray rail tunnel at Yenikapı in 2004-2013 uncovered its quays and 37 shipwrecks of the 5th to 11th centuries, along with Neolithic remains.

monuments.name: Harbour of Julian (Harbour of Sophia)

phases.t: rebuilt by Justin II as the Harbour of Sophia

monuments.summary: A harbour on the Marmara shore built by Julian in 362, rebuilt by Justin II and renamed after his wife Sophia; later known as the Kontoskalion. Its basin is the Kadırga quarter.

monuments.name: Neorion
monuments.summary: The oldest harbour of Byzantium on the Golden Horn, the dockyard of the Greek city, continued in use for shipbuilding and trade near modern Bahçekapı.

monuments.name: Prosphorion
monuments.summary: The harbour of Byzantium on the Golden Horn below the acropolis, near modern Sirkeci, where provisions were landed.

monuments.name: Strategion
monuments.summary: The parade ground of Byzantium near the Golden Horn, embellished by Constantine with statues, and the Strategion baths lay nearby.

monuments.name: Kynegion
monuments.summary: An amphitheatre built by Septimius Severus below the acropolis, used in Byzantine times for executions.

monuments.name: Column of the Goths
monuments.summary: A granite column on the acropolis (Gülhane Park) with the inscription FORTUNAE REDUCI OB DEVICTOS GOTHOS, one of the oldest Roman monuments standing in the city, attributed either to Claudius II after Naissus (269) or to Constantine's Gothic victory of 332.

monuments.name: Palace of Lausus
monuments.summary: The residence of Lausus, grand chamberlain of Theodosius II, NW of the Hippodrome, with a rotunda that housed a collection of Greek masterpieces including Pheidias' Zeus of Olympia, Praxiteles' Aphrodite of Knidos and Lysippus' Kairos. All perished in the fire of 475.

monuments.name: Palace of Antiochus (St Euphemia)

phases.t: converted into the church of St Euphemia

monuments.summary: The palace of the Persian eunuch Antiochus, guardian of the young Theodosius II, west of the Hippodrome, with a hexagonal hall later converted into the church of St Euphemia, which received her relics in the late 7th century.

monuments.name: Blachernae Palace
monuments.summary: An imperial residence by the Blachernae shrine at the NW corner of the city, begun under Anastasius I around 500 for visits to the church. The Komnenoi made it their main palace in the 12th century. The Tekfur Sarayı (late 13th century) is its surviving part.

monuments.name: Wall of Heraclius (Blachernae)
monuments.summary: A single wall built by Heraclius in 627 after the Avar-Persian siege of 626 to bring the Blachernae church, which had lain outside the defences, within the city.

monuments.name: Hebdomon

phases.t: church of St John the Baptist

monuments.summary: The suburb at the seventh milestone on the Marmara with a parade ground (Kampos) and tribunal where armies acclaimed emperors: Valens (364), Arcadius (383), Theodosius II (402), Leo I (457), Basiliscus (475) and Phocas (602). Theodosius I built the church of St John the Baptist here for the Baptist's head (391).

monuments.name: Theodosian Land Walls
monuments.summary: Built in 408-413 under the praetorian prefect Anthemius for the young Theodosius II, about 1.5 km west of Constantine's line, running 5.7 km from the Marmara to the Golden Horn: an inner wall about 5 m thick and 12 m high with 96 towers, an outer wall with its own towers, a terrace and a moat about 20 m wide. The earthquake of 26 January 447, with Attila approaching, brought down 57 towers; the prefect Constantine rebuilt them in about 60 days with the help of the circus factions. They resisted the Avars and Persians (626) and the Arabs (674-678, 717-718), and fell only to the cannon of Mehmed II on 29 May 1453.

monuments.name: Sea Walls
monuments.summary: Walls along the Marmara and the Golden Horn completed in 439 by the prefect Cyrus of Panopolis after Vandal piracy made a seaborne threat real, about 8 km on the Marmara and 5.6 km on the Golden Horn. Theophilos rebuilt much of them in the 9th century. The Crusaders broke in on the Golden Horn side in 1204.

monuments.name: Constantinian Wall
monuments.summary: Constantine's land wall, built 324-c.336 about 2.8 km west of the Severan wall, enclosing seven hills and quintupling the area of Byzantium. Superseded by the Theodosian walls, it decayed and was badly damaged in the earthquake of 557; no trace survives above ground and its course is conjectural.

monuments.name: Golden Gate
monuments.summary: A triple triumphal arch of marble faced with gilded bronze, later built into the Theodosian walls as the ceremonial entrance at the south end of the Mese. Its lost bronze inscription read that 'Theodosius adorns these places after the tyrant's doom', which points either to Theodosius I after Magnus Maximus (388) or to Theodosius II after John (425). Mehmed II built the Yedikule fortress round it in 1458.

monuments.name: Gate of Charisius (Edirnekapı)
monuments.summary: The gate at the highest point of the land walls, where the northern branch of the Mese left the city for Adrianople. Mehmed II entered the city through it on 29 May 1453.

monuments.name: Gate of St Romanus (Topkapı)
monuments.summary: The gate in the Lycus valley section (Mesoteichion), the weakest part of the walls, where the main Ottoman bombardment fell in 1453 and Constantine XI died fighting nearby.

monuments.name: Gate of Rhegion (Mevlevihane Kapısı)
monuments.summary: A military gate of the land walls bearing the inscriptions of the 447 rebuilding: in Latin, 'By Theodosius' orders, in less than two months, Constantine triumphantly built these strong walls; scarcely could Pallas have built so firm a citadel so quickly', with a Greek counterpart.

monuments.name: Gate of Pege (Silivrikapı)
monuments.summary: The gate named for the nearby spring shrine of the Theotokos Pege, through which Alexios Strategopoulos' troops slipped in to retake the city from the Latins in 1261.
